title: Chemical Plant Design and Environmental Impact
topicTitle: Stages in producing a new product; economics of production; running a chemical plant; continuous and batch processing; environmental impact of the chemical industry
notes: **New product development stages:** (1) Discovery — identifying a target molecule or process in the laboratory. (2) Laboratory synthesis — optimising reaction conditions (temperature, solvent, catalyst, concentration) on a gram scale. (3) Pilot plant — scaling up to kilogram quantities in a dedicated facility to test feasibility, safety, and equipment requirements. (4) Process optimisation — refining yield, selectivity, and purity; reducing cost and waste. (5) Commercial production — building a full-scale plant with capacity of tonnes to millions of tonnes per year. (6) Market launch — distribution and quality control.

**Pilot plant design:** a pilot plant typically operates at 10-100 kg per batch to bridge the gap between laboratory (grams) and commercial (tonnes) scale. It reveals scaling issues such as heat transfer limitations, mixing inefficiencies, and safety hazards that are not apparent at lab scale. For exothermic reactions, heat removal becomes increasingly difficult as volume increases (heat generation scales with volume, heat removal with surface area).

**Continuous processing:** reactants are fed continuously into the reactor, and products are removed continuously. Used for high-volume commodities: ammonia synthesis (Haber process), sulfuric acid (Contact process), ethylene production (steam cracking), petroleum refining. Advantages: consistent product quality, lower operating cost per unit, easier automation and control, better heat integration. Disadvantages: high capital cost, inflexible to product changes, difficult to clean between runs.

**Batch processing:** a fixed quantity of reactants is charged into the reactor, the reaction proceeds for a set time, then products are discharged. The reactor is cleaned before the next batch. Used for pharmaceuticals, specialty chemicals, dyes, pigments, and fine chemicals. Advantages: flexibility to switch products, easier to handle viscous or slurry reactions, lower capital cost for small volumes. Disadvantages: higher labour cost, inconsistent quality between batches, downtime for cleaning.

**Economics of chemical production:** key cost components include: (1) Raw material cost — typically 40-60% of total production cost. (2) Energy cost — heating, cooling, compression, and pumping (10-20%). (3) Capital cost — depreciation of plant and equipment (10-15%). (4) Labour — typically 5-10% for automated plants. (5) Waste treatment and disposal — increasingly significant (5-15%). (6) Overheads — maintenance, insurance, administration. Profitability depends on margin between production cost and market price.

**Capital vs operating cost:** capital cost (CAPEX) includes land, buildings, reactors, heat exchangers, piping, instrumentation, and environmental controls. It can range from $10 million for a small specialty plant to $10 billion for an integrated petrochemical complex. Operating cost (OPEX) includes raw materials, energy, labour, and maintenance. Large continuous plants achieve lower OPEX per unit through economies of scale.

**Environmental impact — air pollution:** chemical plants emit $SO_2$ (from sulfuric acid production and sulfide ore roasting), $NO_x$ (from high-temperature processes and ammonia oxidation), particulate matter (from solid handling and drying), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from storage and transfer operations. Scrubbers (wet and dry), electrostatic precipitators, and catalytic converters are used to control emissions.

**Environmental impact — water pollution:** industrial effluents contain dissolved salts, heavy metals (Hg, Pb, Cd, Cr), organic toxins (phenols, pesticides, solvents), and thermal pollution (hot water discharge). Treatment involves neutralisation, precipitation, activated carbon adsorption, biological treatment (activated sludge), and reverse osmosis. Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) systems recover all water for reuse.

**Environmental impact — solid waste:** slag from metal processing, spent catalysts, filter cakes, and sludge from effluent treatment. Hazardous waste must be stabilised (e.g., cement solidification), incinerated at high temperature, or sent to secure landfills. Some waste streams are now valorised — fly ash from power plants is used in cement production; spent catalysts are refined to recover precious metals.

**Green chemistry in plant design:** modern plants incorporate green chemistry principles: catalytic processes replace stoichiometric reagents, solvent-free or water-based reactions replace organic solvents, renewable feedstocks replace petroleum, and process integration (heat exchanger networks) minimises energy use. The concept of 'benign by design' aims to eliminate hazards rather than control them after they are created.

**Case study — phosgene production:** phosgene ($COCl_2$) is a highly toxic gas used to make polycarbonates, polyurethanes, and agrochemicals. Modern plants use in-situ generation (reacting $CO$ and $Cl_2$ over activated carbon catalyst at 50-150°C) rather than storage, minimising the quantity of phosgene present at any time. Continuous flow microreactors further reduce the inventory and improve safety.
confusion: Continuous vs batch — Continuous processing is NOT simply 'faster batch processing.' It is fundamentally different: continuous plants run 24/7 with steady-state operation, while batch plants cycle through charge-reaction-discharge-clean. A continuous plant for 10,000 tonnes/year may be physically smaller than a batch plant for the same output because it eliminates downtime between batches.

Pilot plant vs laboratory — A pilot plant is NOT just a bigger lab. It uses actual process equipment (industrial-scale reactors, heat exchangers, pumps) to reveal engineering issues like pressure drop, mixing time, heat transfer coefficients, and material compatibility that cannot be studied in glassware. Lab scale is typically grams; pilot scale is kilograms; commercial scale is tonnes.

Atom economy vs yield — Yield measures how much product you actually get from a reaction. Atom economy measures what fraction of the reactant atoms end up in the desired product versus waste. A Wittig reaction might have 90% yield but only 30% atom economy because the phosphine oxide byproduct is wasted. A rearrangement reaction has 100% atom economy by definition.

Scrubber vs filter — A scrubber removes gaseous pollutants by absorbing them into a liquid (e.g., caustic scrubber removes $HCl$ gas). A filter (or electrostatic precipitator) removes particulate matter (solid or liquid droplets) from gas streams. Both are air pollution control devices but address different types of emissions.

Green chemistry vs end-of-pipe treatment — Green chemistry prevents pollution at the source by redesigning processes to avoid hazardous substances. End-of-pipe treatment deals with waste after it is created (e.g., treating effluent before discharge). Green chemistry is preferred because it is more sustainable and often more economical in the long run.
practice: A chemical plant produces 50,000 tonnes/year of a specialty chemical via a 3-step batch synthesis with yields of 85%, 78%, and 92% respectively. Calculate the overall yield and the annual raw material requirement (assuming 1:1 stoichiometry). If the same process were run continuously with improved catalysts giving 95%, 90%, and 96% yields, what would the new overall yield be?

Compare the economics of a batch plant (10,000 tonnes/year, 3 batches/day, 300 days/year) versus a continuous plant (same output, 24/7 operation) for a pharmaceutical intermediate. Consider capital cost, operating cost, labour, downtime, and quality consistency. Which would you recommend and why?

A sulfuric acid plant using the Contact process emits $SO_2$ at a rate of 50 kg/hour. Calculate the mass of limestone ($CaCO_3$) required in a wet scrubber to absorb this $SO_2$ completely, assuming 95% scrubber efficiency. The reaction is: $CaCO_3 + SO_2 \rightarrow CaSO_3 + CO_2$.

Design a simple mass balance for a batch reactor producing polyethylene terephthalate (PET) from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol. If you start with 1,000 kg of each reactant, calculate the theoretical yield of PET and the mass of water produced. What is the atom economy of this condensation polymerisation?

Evaluate the environmental impact of producing 1 tonne of chlorine via three different methods: (a) mercury cell electrolysis, (b) diaphragm cell electrolysis, (c) membrane cell electrolysis. Compare them on: energy consumption (kWh/tonne $Cl_2$), mercury pollution, asbestos use (diaphragm), product purity, and compliance with the Minamata Convention on mercury.
universalFacts: The world's largest chemical company (BASF) produced over $85 billion in revenue in 2023 and operates integrated production sites (Verbund) where energy and material streams are optimised across multiple processes.
The total worldwide production of the top 20 bulk chemicals exceeded $2 trillion in 2023. Ethylene, sulfuric acid, and propylene consistently rank among the top three by volume.

The chemical industry generates approximately 1.5 billion tonnes of waste annually, but modern regulations and green chemistry have reduced the toxicity and volume of waste per unit of product by over 60% since 1980.

The concept of 'process safety management' (PSM) requires chemical plants to conduct Process Hazard Analyses (PHA) using methods like HAZOP (Hazard and Operability Study) to identify and mitigate risks before they cause accidents.

The EPA's ChemRing programme and the EU's REACH regulation require manufacturers to test the safety of chemicals before they enter the market, fundamentally changing how new products are developed and evaluated in the 21st century.
